stem: You run `docker pull nginx` with no registry, namespace or tag. Which fully qualified reference does Docker pull?

options.text: `registry.docker.io/nginx/nginx:stable`
options.why: There is no `nginx` namespace or `stable` default; Docker fills in `library` and `latest`.

options.text: `docker.io/library/nginx:latest`
options.why: Docker Hub is the default registry, `library` is the namespace of Official Images, and `latest` is the default tag.

options.text: `localhost/nginx:latest` from a local registry
options.why: Docker never defaults to a local registry; an unqualified name means Docker Hub.

options.text: `docker.io/nginx:newest` resolved by date
options.why: No tag means the literal tag `latest`, not the most recent push.

explanation: Docker normalises short names: no registry host means `docker.io`, a single path component means the `library` namespace used by Docker Official Images, and no tag means `:latest`. `latest` is just a tag name chosen by convention; it is not guaranteed to be the newest image.

stem: Once a tag such as `myapp:1.4` has been pushed to a registry, the registry guarantees it will always point to the same image.

options.text: True
options.why: Tags are mutable pointers unless the registry is configured to make them immutable.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: anyone with push access can move a tag to a new manifest; only a digest identifies fixed content.

explanation: A tag is a human-friendly, movable label. Pushing a new image with the same tag simply repoints it. Content is fixed only when you reference it by digest (`myapp@sha256:…`) or enable tag immutability where the registry offers it, for example in Amazon ECR.
reference: Docker docs: Image tags and digests

stem: Which statement best describes the difference between an image and a container?

options.text: An image is a running process; a container is the file it was started from
options.why: That reverses the two: the image is the template and the container is the running instance.

options.text: A container is a compressed copy of an image used only for distribution
options.why: Distribution uses images; containers are not a transport format.

options.text: A container is an image plus a writable layer, config and a process
options.why: Many containers can run from one read-only image, each with its own thin writable layer.

options.text: They are the same thing; Docker uses both names interchangeably
options.why: They are distinct objects with separate commands, such as `docker image ls` and `docker ps`.

explanation: An image is an immutable stack of read-only layers plus configuration. Running it creates a container: a new writable layer on top, runtime settings (network, mounts, limits) and a process. Deleting the container discards that writable layer, while the image is untouched and can start more containers.
reference: Docker docs: What is an image?

stem: Image and layer digests have the form `<algorithm>:<hex>`. Type the hash algorithm Docker and OCI registries use for them by default.
explanation: Digests look like `sha256:4c0f…`. The digest is the SHA-256 hash of the content (a manifest, config or layer blob), so identical bytes always produce the same digest. That is what makes images content-addressable and lets registries and hosts deduplicate layers.

stem: Match each registry with the shape of its image references.

options.text: `ghcr.io/OWNER/IMAGE:TAG`
`ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com/REPO:TAG`
`REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/REPO/IMAGE:TAG`
`NAME.azurecr.io/REPO:TAG`

explanation: For any registry other than Docker Hub, the first component of the reference is the registry host. GHCR uses `ghcr.io`, ECR uses an account- and region-specific host, Artifact Registry uses a regional `docker.pkg.dev` host plus project and repository, and ACR uses `<registry-name>.azurecr.io`.
reference: Registry documentation: GHCR, ECR, Artifact Registry, ACR

stem: After many rebuilds of `app:dev`, `docker image ls` shows several `<none>:<none>` entries. What does `docker image prune` (without `-a`) remove?

options.text: Every image that no running container uses, tagged or not
options.why: That is `docker image prune -a`, which also removes tagged images with no containers.

options.text: Dangling images: untagged images no container references
options.why: Each rebuild moved the `app:dev` tag, leaving the old image untagged and dangling.

options.text: All images older than 24 hours, whatever their tags
options.why: Pruning by age needs an explicit `--filter until=…`.

options.text: Only stopped containers, leaving every image in place
options.why: Removing stopped containers is `docker container prune`.

explanation: When you rebuild with the same tag, the tag moves to the new image and the previous one becomes dangling (`<none>:<none>`). `docker image prune` deletes only those dangling images. Adding `-a` widens it to every image not used by a container, which can remove base images you will need to pull again.

stem: Which three things make up a container image as stored in a registry? (Choose three.)

options.text: A manifest listing the config and layer blobs by digest
options.why: The manifest is the entry point the client fetches first.

options.text: A JSON config with entrypoint, environment and layer diff IDs
options.why: The config carries runtime defaults and history, and its digest is the image ID.

options.text: Compressed filesystem layers, each stored as a blob
options.why: Each layer is a tar archive of filesystem changes, usually gzip- or zstd-compressed.

options.text: A snapshot of the memory of a running container
options.why: Images contain files and metadata, never process memory.

options.text: The data from every named volume the app has written to
options.why: Volumes live outside images and are never pushed with them.

explanation: Per the OCI image spec an image is a manifest that references one config blob and an ordered list of layer blobs, all by digest. Running state such as memory, and data in volumes, are not part of the image.

stem: Which command lists an image's layers with the instruction that created each one and its size?

options.text: `docker image ls --layers app:1.0`
options.why: `docker image ls` lists images; it has no layer breakdown flag.

options.text: `docker container inspect app:1.0`
options.why: That inspects containers, not images, and returns JSON without per-layer sizes.

options.text: `docker history app:1.0`
options.why: It shows one row per layer, with the creating instruction and its size.

options.text: `docker image diff app:1.0`
options.why: `docker diff` compares a container's filesystem with its image; there is no `image diff`.

explanation: `docker history` (also `docker image history`) shows the image's history entries, newest first: the instruction that created each layer, when, and how large it is. Steps such as `ENV` or `CMD` show a size of 0 B because they change only the config.

stem: Staging and production both run `myapp:latest`. A bug appears only in production, and `docker image inspect` shows different image IDs on the two hosts. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Production's Docker daemon applied its own compression, changing the image
options.why: Compression doesn't change what runs, and the image ID is the digest of the config.

options.text: `latest` was re-pushed between the two pulls, so the images differ
options.why: A tag is a moving pointer, so two pulls at different times can resolve to different images.

options.text: Image IDs are random per host, so the difference is expected and harmless
options.why: Image IDs are content-derived; the same image has the same ID everywhere.

options.text: Production pulled from a mirror that edits images to add security patches
options.why: Mirrors and caches serve the same content-addressed blobs; they don't rewrite images.

explanation: Deploying a mutable tag means each host gets whatever the tag pointed to when it pulled. Use an immutable tag per build (for example the git SHA) and pin deploys by digest (`myapp@sha256:…`), so every environment runs exactly the same bytes.
reference: Docker docs: Image tags and digests

stem: You need to move an image to an air-gapped server and keep its tags, layers and history. Which pair of commands should you use?

options.text: `docker export` on the source host and `docker import` on the target host
options.why: Export flattens a container's filesystem and drops the image's tags, history and config.

options.text: `docker commit` on the source and `docker run` on the target
options.why: Commit creates a new image from a container; it doesn't transfer anything.

options.text: `docker save -o app.tar app:1.0`, then `docker load -i app.tar`
options.why: Save writes the image with all layers, config and tags; load restores it as-is.

options.text: `docker cp` the image directory and restart the daemon
options.why: Copying daemon storage by hand is unsupported and depends on the storage driver.

explanation: `docker save` produces a tar of one or more images (layers, config, manifest and tag references) that `docker load` restores intact. `docker export` works on a container: it outputs a single flat filesystem tar, and `docker import` turns that into a one-layer image without the original `CMD`, `ENV`, `ENTRYPOINT` or history.

stem: Which two tagging practices make deployments reproducible and traceable? (Choose two.)

options.text: Tag every build with an immutable identifier such as the git commit SHA
options.why: A unique tag per build never moves, so it always names the same image.

options.text: Deploy by digest, keeping a semver tag for people to read
options.why: The digest pins exact content, and the version tag stays human-readable.

options.text: Deploy `:latest` so every host always runs the newest build
options.why: Hosts pull at different times and may run different builds under one name.

options.text: Re-push fixes under the existing release tag to avoid a new version
options.why: Silently moving a release tag breaks traceability and caching assumptions.

options.text: Use the build date as the only tag so images sort by age
options.why: Two builds on one day collide, and dates say nothing about the source.

explanation: Good practice: one immutable tag per build (git SHA or build number), optional moving convenience tags such as `1.4` or `stable` for humans, and deployments that reference the digest. Never reuse a release tag for different content.

stem: On an Apple Silicon Mac you run `docker pull python:3.13-slim` with no extra flags. The official image is published for several architectures. What do you get?

options.text: The `linux/amd64` variant, emulated, because it is the default platform
options.why: Docker picks the variant matching the host unless told otherwise.

options.text: The `linux/arm64` variant, chosen from the image index
options.why: The tag points to an index, and the client picks the manifest for its platform.

options.text: Every architecture's layers, so the image runs anywhere
options.why: Only the selected platform's manifest and layers are downloaded.

options.text: An error asking you to choose a platform with `--platform`
options.why: Multi-platform tags resolve automatically; `--platform` only overrides the choice.

explanation: Multi-platform tags point to an image index (manifest list) with one entry per platform. The client chooses the entry matching the daemon's platform, here `linux/arm64`, and pulls only that image. Use `--platform linux/amd64` to deliberately pull another variant, which then runs under emulation.

stem: Put the steps of `docker pull ghcr.io/acme/api:2.1` in the order they happen for a multi-platform image.

options.text: Authenticate with the registry and obtain a token for that repository
Download the config and any layer blobs not already stored locally
Fetch the manifest for tag `2.1`, which is an image index
Verify each blob against its digest and unpack the layers
Parse the reference into registry host, repository and tag
Select the platform manifest matching the host from the index

explanation: The client resolves the reference, gets a bearer token scoped to the repository, fetches the tag's manifest (an index for multi-platform images), picks the matching platform manifest, then downloads only the blobs it doesn't already have. Every blob is checked against its digest before use.

stem: On a Linux server with no credential helper configured, how does `docker login` store the password or token?

options.text: Encrypted with a key derived from the server's machine ID
options.why: Docker applies no encryption when no credential store or helper is configured.

options.text: Only in memory until the daemon restarts, after which it is discarded
options.why: Credentials persist on disk so later pulls and pushes work.

options.text: Base64-encoded, not encrypted, in `~/.docker/config.json`
options.why: Base64 is just an encoding, which is why Docker warns about unencrypted storage.

options.text: In the registry, which then trusts the host by IP address
options.why: Registries authenticate each request; they don't remember hosts.

explanation: Without `credsStore` or `credHelpers` in `config.json`, credentials go under `auths` as base64 of `user:password`, which anyone who can read the file can decode. Configure a credential helper (the OS keychain, `pass`, or a cloud helper such as `docker-credential-ecr-login`) to keep secrets out of the file.

stem: If two images on a host are built `FROM` the same base image, the base layers are stored only once on disk.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: layers are content-addressed, so identical layers are shared between images.

options.text: False
options.why: Identical layers have identical digests and are stored once, then shared.

explanation: Layers are identified by digest, so a layer present in several images is downloaded and stored once. `docker system df -v` shows each image's unique size next to its shared size. That sharing is why a common base image makes pulls of later images fast.
reference: Docker docs: Storage drivers (images and layers)

stem: Your CI runners share one outbound IP and pull public base images from Docker Hub without logging in. Builds start failing with `toomanyrequests`. What is the best fix?

options.text: Pull with `--platform` so each architecture counts as one pull
options.why: Pull counting doesn't depend on that flag, and multi-arch pulls count per architecture.

options.text: Retry failed pulls in a tight loop until one gets through
options.why: Retries consume more of the limit and stretch out the lockout.

options.text: Authenticate pulls, or route them through a mirror or pull-through cache
options.why: Logged-in pulls count against the account's higher limit, and a cache avoids repeat pulls.

options.text: Switch from version tags to `:latest`, which isn't subject to the rate limit
options.why: Every tag counts the same; `latest` has no exemption.

explanation: Docker Hub limits pulls per 6 hours: unauthenticated pulls count per IPv4 address or IPv6 /64 subnet, while authenticated accounts get their plan's limit. At the time of writing that is 100 per 6 hours anonymous, 200 for Personal and unlimited for paid plans. Shared CI IPs hit the anonymous limit quickly. Log in, use a registry mirror or pull-through cache, or copy base images into your own registry.
reference: Docker docs: Docker Hub pull usage and limits

stem: Type the flag that makes `docker pull` fetch a specific platform variant, for example `linux/amd64`, instead of the host's own.
explanation: `docker pull --platform linux/amd64 image:tag` selects that entry from the image index. The same flag exists on `docker run` and `docker buildx build`. On a host with a different architecture the container then runs under emulation (QEMU) if it is available.

stem: A team switches its base image from `debian:bookworm-slim` to `alpine`. A prebuilt Linux binary copied into the image now fails with `exec ./tool: no such file or directory`, though `ls` shows the file is there. Why?

options.text: Alpine mounts `/` read-only, so newly copied files are hidden from the shell
options.why: Alpine's root filesystem is writable in containers, and the file is visible.

options.text: It links against glibc, but Alpine uses musl, so the loader is missing
options.why: The kernel can't find the ELF interpreter, which is reported as "no such file".

options.text: Alpine uses a different CPU architecture from Debian images
options.why: Both are available for the same architectures; the issue is the C library.

options.text: BusyBox `sh` refuses to run binaries that are larger than 1 MB
options.why: There is no such size limit.

explanation: Alpine uses musl libc, while most prebuilt Linux binaries expect glibc and its loader (`/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`). When the loader named in the ELF header is missing, `exec` fails with "no such file or directory", which is confusing because the binary itself exists. Use a glibc-based image (debian-slim, distroless), a static binary, or a musl build.
reference: Alpine Linux docs: Running glibc programs

stem: Match each command with the information it is best for.

options.text: Local image metadata as JSON: config, ID, RepoDigests
Layer-by-layer history with creating instructions and sizes
The remote manifest or index, including every platform
Local images listed with their repository digests

explanation: `inspect` reads local metadata, `history` explains how the layers were built, `buildx imagetools inspect` queries the registry for the manifest or index without pulling, and `image ls --digests` shows which registry digest each local tag came from.
reference: Docker docs: docker buildx imagetools inspect

stem: A deployment pins `api@sha256:ab12…`, and that digest belongs to a multi-platform image index. Hosts are a mix of amd64 and arm64. What happens on pull?

options.text: Every host pulls the amd64 image, because a digest pins one exact platform
options.why: An index digest pins the whole index, and each host still selects its own entry.

options.text: The pull fails, because digests may only reference single-platform image manifests
options.why: Indexes are content-addressed too and can be pulled by digest.

options.text: Each host pulls its own platform's image, and both stay pinned to that index
options.why: The index and the manifests it lists are fixed by the digest, so neither variant can drift.

options.text: Each host pulls the newest image for its platform, ignoring the index
options.why: Pinning by digest exists precisely to stop drift.

explanation: Pinning a multi-platform image by its index digest is the usual best practice. The index content, and therefore the digests of every platform manifest it references, are fixed, while each host still resolves its own platform. Pinning a platform manifest digest instead would force that one architecture everywhere.

stem: For the same local image, `docker image inspect` shows an `Id` of `sha256:9f1c…` but a `RepoDigests` entry of `app@sha256:4d7e…`. Assuming the classic image store, why do they differ?

options.text: The Id hashes the compressed layers and RepoDigests hashes the uncompressed ones
options.why: Neither value is a hash of the layers themselves.

options.text: The Id hashes the image config; the repo digest hashes the manifest
options.why: Different JSON documents give different hashes, and registries address manifests.

options.text: The repo digest changes on every pull, but the Id stays stable
options.why: Both are content hashes and are stable for the same content.

options.text: Docker truncates the Id to 12 characters, so the two can never match
options.why: Truncation is only for display; the full values differ for a real reason.

explanation: With the classic image store, the image ID is the SHA-256 of the image config JSON. The manifest that registries serve references that config plus the layers, and its own hash is the repo digest you use in `name@sha256:…`. Always pin the repo digest, because it is what registries resolve.
reference: OCI Image Spec: Manifest and Config

stem: You rebuild the same commit with no source changes and push again, and the image gets a new digest. Which two causes are most likely? (Choose two.)

options.text: The config's creation timestamp changed, so the config and manifest hashes change
options.why: Timestamps in the config feed straight into the digest.

options.text: Files in a layer got new modification times, so the layer tarball differs
options.why: Layer digests hash the tar bytes, including file mtimes.

options.text: Registries add a random salt to every manifest they receive
options.why: Registries store manifests byte for byte; digests are deterministic.

options.text: The tag name is part of the digest, and the tag was re-applied
options.why: Tags point to manifests and are not part of the hashed content.

options.text: Pushing always recompresses layers with a new random seed
options.why: Compression is deterministic for identical input.

explanation: A digest is a hash of exact bytes. Build timestamps in the image config and file modification times inside layer tarballs make otherwise identical builds differ. Reproducible builds pin these, for example with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, which BuildKit honours.
reference: Docker docs: Reproducible builds with SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH

stem: A developer builds an image on an Apple Silicon Mac with a plain `docker build` and pushes it. On the amd64 production servers the container exits immediately with `exec format error`. What is the right fix?

options.text: Add `--privileged` to `docker run` so the kernel can run any binary
options.why: Privileges don't change which CPU architectures the kernel can execute.

options.text: Rebuild with `--platform linux/amd64`, or push a multi-platform image
options.why: The pushed image was arm64-only; production needs an amd64 variant.

options.text: Change the base image tag from `latest` to a pinned version
options.why: The base tag isn't the problem; the CPU architecture of the build output is.

options.text: Re-push with `docker push --platform all` to convert the existing image
options.why: Pushing can't convert binaries from one architecture to another.

explanation: A plain build targets the builder's own platform, here `linux/arm64`. An amd64 host can't execute those binaries, which surfaces as `exec format error`. Build with `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push` to publish an index containing both, or target the production platform explicitly.

stem: On a build server you run `docker image prune -a` while no containers are running. What does it remove?

options.text: Only dangling `<none>` images, keeping everything that has a tag
options.why: That is the behaviour without `-a`.

options.text: Only images older than the build cache retention period
options.why: Age filtering requires `--filter until=…`.

options.text: Every image not used by a container, tagged ones included
options.why: With no containers running, that can be every image on the host.

options.text: The build cache, but no images
options.why: The build cache is cleaned with `docker builder prune`.

explanation: `-a` changes the rule from "dangling" to "unused by any container". On a build host with no running containers it can delete every base image, so the next build pulls everything again, perhaps against rate limits. Prefer filters such as `--filter until=168h`, or prune only dangling images.

stem: Deleting a tag, or even a manifest, from a self-hosted `registry:2` immediately frees the disk space used by its layers.

options.text: True
options.why: Layer blobs remain until a separate garbage-collection run removes the unreferenced ones.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: deletion only unlinks the manifest, and space comes back after garbage collection.

explanation: In the open-source distribution registry, deleting a manifest removes the reference, but the blobs stay because other manifests may share them. You must run `registry garbage-collect`, ideally with the registry read-only or stopped, to remove unreferenced blobs. Managed registries such as ECR or GHCR handle this themselves.

stem: A service runs `docker run -d api:stable`. After the team pushes a new `api:stable`, restarting the service with the same command still runs the old version. Why?

options.text: `docker run` always pulls, so the registry must still be serving the old image
options.why: By default `docker run` does not pull when a local image with that tag exists.

options.text: The default pull policy is `missing`, so the cached tag is reused
options.why: Use `--pull=always` or an explicit `docker pull` to refresh the tag.

options.text: Tags are resolved only once per host and cached permanently
options.why: Pulling again re-resolves the tag; nothing is cached permanently.

options.text: The daemon refuses to replace an image while any container is using it
options.why: A pull can retag the new image even while old containers keep running the old one.

explanation: `docker run` uses `--pull=missing` by default: it pulls only if the image isn't available locally. A moved tag therefore isn't noticed. Pull first, use `--pull=always`, or better, deploy immutable tags or digests so the version change is explicit.

stem: Which three statements about distroless base images (such as `gcr.io/distroless/static` or `base`) are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: They omit a shell and package manager, so `docker exec … sh` fails
options.why: Only the app and its runtime dependencies are included.

options.text: Fewer packages mean a smaller attack surface and fewer CVEs to triage
options.why: Less software in the image means less to patch.

options.text: Debugging usually needs a `:debug` variant or an attached debug container
options.why: The debug variants add BusyBox for interactive troubleshooting.

options.text: They are based on musl, like Alpine, so glibc binaries won't run
options.why: The distroless base images are Debian-based and use glibc.

options.text: They are guaranteed to have zero known vulnerabilities
options.why: Fewer packages reduce findings, but nothing guarantees zero.

explanation: Distroless images contain the minimum needed to run an app: no shell, no package manager, and Debian-derived glibc variants for dynamic binaries. That shrinks size and attack surface, but changes how you debug. Use the `:debug` tags or an ephemeral debug container.

stem: Docker Hub counts pulls per architecture for multi-platform images. A CI job, unauthenticated, runs `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64` with `FROM node:22-slim` and no cache. How many Hub pulls does that build use for the base image?

options.text: One, because a single tag was requested
options.why: Each platform resolves to a separate platform manifest, and each counts.

options.text: Two: one pull of the base image per target platform
options.why: One manifest pull is counted for each architecture built.

options.text: Zero, because buildx pulls don't count toward limits
options.why: BuildKit pulls are ordinary registry pulls and are counted.

options.text: Four, one per platform for the manifest and one for the layers
options.why: Pulls are counted per manifest, not per layer download.

explanation: Docker Hub defines a pull as a manifest request, and a multi-architecture pull counts once per architecture. Version checks that only verify a tag exists don't count. Multi-platform builds therefore use limits faster; authenticate and cache base images.
reference: Docker docs: Docker Hub pull usage and limits

stem: Docker treats the first part of a reference as a registry host only if it contains a `.` or a `:` or is `localhost`. For `team/app:1.0`, which registry host is used? Type the host name.
explanation: `team` contains no dot or colon and isn't `localhost`, so it is a namespace on the default registry, Docker Hub (`docker.io`, served from `registry-1.docker.io`). By contrast `myreg:5000/app` and `registry.local/app` name explicit hosts. This rule is why private registries need a dotted or ported hostname.
reference: Docker docs: docker image tag (image name format)

stem: A teammate fixed a bug inside a running container and then ran `docker commit` to publish the result as `app:hotfix`. Why is this a poor way to ship images?

options.text: Committed images can only run on the host that created them, so they can't ship
options.why: Committed images can be pushed and run anywhere, which is part of the risk.

options.text: There's no Dockerfile to rebuild or review it, and it may hold leftover secrets
options.why: The image captures whatever happened to be in the container, with no recorded recipe.

options.text: Committed images don't get a digest, so they can't be pinned
options.why: A committed image has a config and manifest digest like any other.

options.text: `docker commit` deletes the container's writable layer
options.why: Commit copies the writable layer into a new image; the container is untouched.

explanation: A committed image freezes the container's current state: shell history, caches, temporary credentials and whatever else was changed by hand. Without a Dockerfile and CI build it can't be reproduced, reviewed or patched systematically. Put the fix in the Dockerfile and rebuild.

stem: A deployment manifest uses `image: nginx:1.27@sha256:5f2…`, but the digest belongs to a different nginx release than 1.27. What does Docker pull?

options.text: `nginx:1.27`, because the tag is more specific than the digest
options.why: The tag is not used for resolution when a digest is present.

options.text: The image with that digest; the tag is effectively ignored
options.why: A digest uniquely identifies content, so it takes precedence.

options.text: Nothing: the client rejects references that have both a tag and a digest
options.why: Tag-plus-digest references are allowed.

options.text: Both images, choosing whichever was pushed most recently
options.why: Only one manifest is fetched.

explanation: When a reference has both a tag and a digest, the digest decides what is pulled and the tag is informational. That makes `name:tag@sha256:…` handy for readability, but a stale tag can mislead reviewers. Tools such as Renovate update both together.
reference: Docker docs: Pull an image by digest

stem: Put the steps for publishing `app:1.4` to Amazon ECR and deploying it reproducibly in order.

options.text: Log in to ECR with a token from `aws ecr get-login-password`
Tag the image as `ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com/app:1.4`
Push the tag with `docker push`
Record the pushed digest and deploy `app@sha256:…`

explanation: ECR authentication uses a short-lived password from `aws ecr get-login-password`, piped into `docker login --username AWS`. You tag the image with the registry host and push it, then deploy by the digest that push reports, so every environment runs identical content.
reference: Amazon ECR docs: Pushing a Docker image

stem: Match each base image with the trait that defines it.

options.text: Empty filesystem; suits fully static binaries
musl libc and BusyBox, about 5 MB, `apk` packages
glibc and `apt`, broad compatibility, larger
glibc runtime libraries, no shell or package manager

explanation: `scratch` contains nothing, so only static binaries run on it. Alpine is tiny but uses musl, which affects prebuilt binaries and Python wheels. debian-slim trades size for glibc compatibility and `apt`. Distroless keeps glibc for dynamic binaries but removes the shell and package manager to shrink the attack surface.
reference: Docker Official Images docs; distroless README

stem: Policy says production must run exactly the content that was scanned. A developer re-pushed a patched build under the existing `payments:3.2.0` tag, and some nodes are running the old image. Which control enforces the policy?

options.text: Set `--pull=always` on every node so all nodes converge on the newest `3.2.0`
options.why: That converges on whatever the tag currently points to, which may be unscanned.

options.text: Run a weekly `docker image prune -a` so stale images get removed
options.why: Pruning doesn't stop a tag from being moved to unscanned content.

options.text: Enable tag immutability, and deploy the scanned digest rather than the tag
options.why: Immutability stops re-pushes, and digest pinning ties deploys to scanned bytes.

options.text: Sign the tag, so a moved tag automatically gets re-scanned
options.why: Signatures cover digests; signing doesn't trigger scans or stop re-tagging.

explanation: Two controls close the gap. Registry tag immutability (ECR, ACR and others support it) rejects pushes that would move an existing tag, and deployments reference the digest that was scanned and approved. A moving tag can never guarantee identical content.
reference: Amazon ECR docs: Image tag mutability

stem: Two hosts run `docker pull app:1.0` within the same minute and still end up with different image IDs. Which two explanations are plausible? (Choose two.)

options.text: The hosts have different CPU architectures, so they pulled different entries from the index
options.why: Each platform image has its own config, so its ID differs.

options.text: The tag was re-pushed between the two pulls
options.why: Even a minute is enough for CI to move a tag.

options.text: Image IDs include the host name, so they always differ between machines
options.why: IDs are derived only from content.

options.text: Each daemon decompresses layers differently, changing the ID
options.why: The ID comes from the config, which is identical across daemons.

options.text: Docker Hub returns a randomized manifest to spread load across hosts
options.why: Manifests are content-addressed and served byte for byte.

explanation: Different IDs for one tag mean different content: either the index resolved to different platform images (amd64 and arm64 configs differ), or the tag moved between pulls. Compare `docker image inspect --format '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}} {{.RepoDigests}}'` on both hosts to tell which.

stem: A host has three images. A and B are both built on `base:1` (700 MB) and add unique layers of 200 MB and 100 MB. C is built on `base:2` (700 MB, sharing no layers with `base:1`) and adds a 50 MB layer. Roughly how much disk do these images use in total?

options.text: About 2,450 MB, because each image stores its full stack
options.why: Shared base layers are stored once, not once per image.

options.text: About 1,750 MB: 700 + 200 + 100 for A and B, plus 750 for C
options.why: `base:1` is shared by A and B; `base:2` is separate.

options.text: About 1,050 MB, because all three share one base
options.why: `base:1` and `base:2` have different layers, so nothing is shared between them.

options.text: About 700 MB, because Docker deduplicates every file across images
options.why: Deduplication is per layer, not per file across different layers.

explanation: Layers are shared when their digests match. A and B share `base:1`: 700 + 200 + 100 = 1,000 MB. C needs all of `base:2` plus its own layer: 700 + 50 = 750 MB. The total is about 1,750 MB. Standardising on one base version across services directly saves disk, pull time and bandwidth.

stem: Your team signs images with cosign and verifies them before deploying. Why does cosign sign the manifest digest rather than the tag?

options.text: Tags can't be read through the registry API, so there is nothing to sign
options.why: Tags are fully readable; the problem is that they move.

options.text: A signed tag could later point to unsigned content; a digest names fixed bytes
options.why: The signature has to be bound to the content itself, not a movable pointer.

options.text: Signing a digest makes the image smaller, because the signature replaces layers
options.why: Signatures are stored separately and add a small artifact.

options.text: Registries reject signatures attached to tags
options.why: The design reason is security, not a registry limitation.

explanation: Because tags are mutable, a signature on a tag would vouch for whatever the tag points to later. Cosign signs the manifest digest and stores the signature as an OCI artifact in the same registry. Verification resolves the image to a digest and checks the signature for that digest, so swapping the content breaks verification.

stem: Deployments pin `api@sha256:…`. Weeks later new nodes fail with `manifest unknown` for the pinned digest, although `api:3.4` still pulls fine. ECR has a lifecycle rule that expires untagged images after 14 days. What happened?

options.text: ECR re-signed the image, changing its digest
options.why: ECR doesn't modify stored manifests.

options.text: `3.4` was re-pushed, so the pinned manifest became untagged and expired
options.why: An untagged manifest is exactly what "expire untagged" removes.

options.text: Digest references expire automatically after 14 days in every registry
options.why: Digests don't expire; storage policies delete content.

options.text: The new nodes have a different architecture, so the digest no longer matches
options.why: A platform mismatch gives a platform error, not `manifest unknown`.

explanation: Moving `3.4` to a new build left the old manifest with no tags. The lifecycle rule treats untagged images as garbage and deleted it after 14 days, so anything pinned to that digest can no longer pull it. Use immutable tags, keep tags on deployed digests, or exclude them from lifecycle cleanup.

stem: Adding a new platform (for example `linux/riscv64`) to an existing multi-platform tag changes the digest of the image index, even though the amd64 and arm64 images are unchanged.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the index lists every platform, so new content means a new digest.

options.text: False
options.why: The index document changes when an entry is added, and its hash changes with it.

explanation: An image index is a JSON document that lists a descriptor for each platform manifest. Adding an entry changes the bytes and so the index digest, while each existing platform manifest keeps its own digest. Deployments pinned to the old index digest keep working, and new ones need the new digest to see the extra platform.

stem: You start a container from an image created with `docker export` piped into `docker import`. The original image had `ENTRYPOINT ["node","server.js"]` and `ENV NODE_ENV=production`. What happens?

options.text: It starts normally, because `docker import` restores the original image config
options.why: `docker export` contains only files, so there's no config to restore.

options.text: It fails, because imported images can't be run, only inspected
options.why: Imported images run like any other, given a command.

options.text: No entrypoint or env survive, so `docker run` errors: no command specified
options.why: Export keeps the filesystem and drops every image config value.

options.text: It runs, but the image has twice the original number of layers
options.why: An imported image is a single flattened layer.

explanation: `export` and `import` move a flat root filesystem. The result is a single-layer image with an empty config, so there is no `ENTRYPOINT`, `CMD`, `ENV`, `WORKDIR`, `USER` or exposed ports, and `docker run` fails with no command specified. You must add them back with `docker import --change 'ENTRYPOINT […]'`, or use `save`/`load`, which preserve the config.

stem: A company's CI pulls hundreds of public base images a day and keeps hitting Docker Hub limits. Which three measures address it sustainably? (Choose three.)

options.text: Authenticate CI pulls with a paid organization account
options.why: Paid plans remove the per-6-hour pull limit, subject to fair use.

options.text: Run a pull-through cache or registry mirror in front of Docker Hub
options.why: Repeated pulls of the same image are then served locally.

options.text: Copy approved base images into your own registry and build from there
options.why: Builds then don't depend on Docker Hub at all.

options.text: Build every image for all platforms so the cache warms faster
options.why: More platforms mean more counted pulls, not fewer.

options.text: Use `--pull=always` so builds never use a stale base
options.why: Always pulling increases the number of counted pulls.

explanation: Limits are cut by authenticating, by caching (a `registry-mirrors` entry in `daemon.json`, or a pull-through cache such as ECR's or Harbor's), and by owning copies of your dependencies. Copying base images also speeds builds and makes the supply chain auditable.
reference: Docker docs: Registry mirrors; Docker Hub usage and limits

stem: Base images in your Dockerfiles are pinned like `FROM node:22-slim@sha256:…`. Security asks how you get patched bases without losing reproducibility. Which approach meets both goals?

options.text: Remove the digests and rebuild nightly from the moving tag
options.why: You get patches, but each build becomes non-reproducible.

options.text: Keep the digests and never update them, to guarantee reproducibility
options.why: Builds reproduce, but known CVEs in the base are never fixed.

options.text: Keep the digests and let a bot like Renovate open update PRs
options.why: Every update is explicit, reviewed and tested, then reproducible again.

options.text: Pin only the major version tag, such as `node:22`, since it is immutable
options.why: Major version tags move with every patch release.

explanation: Digest pinning makes each build reproducible. Automated update PRs (Renovate, Dependabot) refresh the digest whenever the upstream tag moves, so patches arrive through normal review and CI. You get both: patched bases and builds you can recreate exactly.
reference: Docker docs: Build best practices (pin base image versions)

stem: `docker buildx imagetools inspect myorg/api:2.0` lists `linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`, and two entries with platform `unknown/unknown`. What are the `unknown/unknown` entries?

options.text: Corrupted manifests left behind by an earlier push that was interrupted midway
options.why: They are valid manifests created on purpose.

options.text: Attestation manifests, such as provenance or SBOM, that BuildKit attached
options.why: They are tagged `unknown/unknown` so clients never pick them to run.

options.text: Images for platforms that the registry doesn't recognise yet
options.why: Real platforms are recorded explicitly, even unusual ones.

options.text: Windows variants, which are always reported as unknown on Linux
options.why: Windows images report `windows/amd64` and similar.

explanation: BuildKit stores build attestations (SLSA provenance by default when pushing, and an SBOM when requested) as extra manifests in the image index. They use the `unknown/unknown` platform so container runtimes never select them to run. Tools that inspect supply-chain metadata read them.

stem: A Python service moved from `python:3.13-slim` to `python:3.13-alpine` to shrink the image. Builds now take 15 minutes instead of 1 and need a compiler. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Alpine's pip is an older release that disables the wheel cache
options.why: Alpine images ship current pip; the issue is wheel compatibility.

options.text: Some packages ship only glibc `manylinux` wheels, so pip compiles them
options.why: Without a matching musl wheel, pip falls back to compiling the source distribution.

options.text: Alpine runs pip under emulation because it targets a different architecture
options.why: The architecture is unchanged; only the C library differs.

options.text: BusyBox limits pip to installing one package at a time
options.why: BusyBox has no say in how pip installs packages.

explanation: Many Python packages publish `manylinux` wheels, which require glibc. On musl-based Alpine pip can use only `musllinux` wheels, so for packages without one it downloads the source distribution and compiles it, which needs a compiler and headers and is slow. The final image can even end up larger. A slim glibc base is usually the better trade-off for Python.
reference: Python Packaging docs: Platform compatibility tags

stem: A security review asks which references make `docker run` execute byte-identical content on every host, no matter what is pushed later. Which two qualify? (Choose two.)

options.text: `app@sha256:<index digest>`
options.why: A digest names fixed content, and an index digest also fixes every platform entry.

options.text: `app:1.4@sha256:<digest>`
options.why: When a digest is present it decides what is pulled; the tag is only informational.

options.text: `app:1.4` in an ECR repository with immutable tags
options.why: Immutability blocks overwrites, but the image can be deleted and the tag pushed again.

options.text: `app:latest` combined with `--pull=always`
options.why: That guarantees the newest content, not identical content.

options.text: `app:1.4` pulled once and then left cached on each host
options.why: Hosts that pull at different times can still get different images.

explanation: Only a digest names immutable content: the registry has to return exactly those bytes or fail the pull. Immutable tags are a strong guard, but they still depend on repository policy, deletions and access control. Tags plus `--pull=always` optimise for freshness, not sameness.
reference: Docker docs: Pull an image by digest
